la:verb:tollo.html:
tollo, sustŭli, sublātum, 3, v. a. (
perf. tollit, : tollisse,) [root Sanscr. tul-, tulajāmi, lift up, weigh; Gr. ταλ-, τελ, in τλῆναι, τάλαντον; cf.: tuli, tlātus (latus), tolerare], to lift or take up, to raise, always with the predom. idea of motion upwards or of removal from a former situation.
To lift up, raise up, elevate, exalt, etc. (syn.: effero, elevo).
Lit.
In gen.: unus erit quem tu tolles in caerula caeli templa, Enn. ap. Müll. (Ann. v. 66 Vahl.): pileum ad caelum tollit, Plaut. Fragm. ap. : fulgor ibi ad caelum se tollit,; for which also: aliquem tollere in caelum,: quem (Herculem) in caelum ista ipsa sustulit fortitudo,; : tollam ego ted in collum,: Phaëthon optavit, ut in currum patris tolleretur: sublatus est,; cf. : aliquem in equum,: quos in crucem sustulit,: aliquem in crucem,, § 13: aquila in sublime sustulit testudinem,: in arduos Tollor Sabinos, et saep.: ut me hic jacentem aliquis tollat,; so, jacentes,: mulum suum tollebat Fufius, lifted up, raised up, Varr. ap. : nequeo caput tollere,: sustulimus manus et ego et Balbus,: manus,: gradum,: scorpius caudā sublatā, Lucil. ap. : lubrica convolvit sublato pectore terga (coluber),: terrā,: de terrā,: se tollere a terrā,: ignis e speculā sublatus,.—
In partic.
Tollere liberos, to take up, i. e. to accept, acknowledge; and so, to raise up, bring up, educate as one's own (from the custom of laying new-born children on the ground at the father's feet; cf. suscipio): quod erit natum, tollito,: puerum,; Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 67 Vahl.): natum filium,: nothum,: puellam,; cf. .—Also of the mother: si quod peperissem, id educarem ac tollerem,.—
Transf., in gen., to get, beget a child: qui ex Fadiā sustulerit liberos,: decessit morbo aquae intercutis, sublato filio Nerone ex Agrippinā, —
Nautical t. t.: tollere ancoras, to lift the anchor, weigh anchor; esp. in part. pass.: sublatis ancoris,; ; . —
Transf. out of the nautical sphere, to break up, proceed: si vultis ancoras tollere,.—
To build, raise, erect: tollam altius tectum,: si juxta habeas aedificia, eaque jure tuo altius tollas,.—
To take on board, carry, of vessels or vehicles: navem, metretas quae trecentas tolleret, parasse,: naves, quae equites sustulerant,: altera navis ducentos ex legione tironum sustulerat,; Auct. B. Afr. 54: tollite me, Teucri,: ut se sublatum in lembum ad Cotym deveheret,: Maecenas me tollere raedā vellet,: Talem te Bacchus ... sustulit in currus,. —
Trop.
To raise, lift, lift up, elevate, set up, etc.: tollitur in caelum clamor exortus utrimque, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 422 Vahl.): clamorem in caelum,: clamores ad sidera,; cf.: clamor magnus se tollit ad auras,rises,: clamor a vigilibus tollitur,: clamorem,: cachinnum,: risum,: litterulae meae tui desiderio oblanguerunt: hac tamen epistulā oculos paulum sustulerunt, have opened

their eyes again, have reanimated them, .—Esp. with animos: ne in secunda tollere animos et in mala demittere, to elevate, Lucil. ap. : animos,; : animos alicui,to raise, excite, animate,: nec dubium est quin omnis Hispania sublatura animos fuerit,; opp. abicere animos,: aliquid dicendo augere et tollere altius (opp. extenuare et abicere),: ad caelum te tollimus verissimis ac justissimis laudibus,: monumentum illud, quod tu tollere laudibus solebas, (14): nostras laudes in astra,: Daphnim tuum ad astra,: tergeminis tollere honoribus,: vos Tempe tollite laudibus, (cf. also Brut. ap. ; v.infra, II. A. 2.): supra modum se tollens oratio,; cf.: se eadem geometria tollit ad rationem usque mundi,; : amicum Tollere (i. q. consolari),to cheer up, console,.—

To take on one, assume, bear, endure: providere non solum quid oneris in praesentia tollant,: at Apollodorus poenas sustulit,. —
To take up a thing from its place, to take away, remove, to bear or carry away, make way with, take away with one (syn.: aufero, adimo).
Lit.
In gen.: frumentum de areā,: solem e mundo tollere videntur, qui amicitiam e vitā tollunt,: ut aliquis nos deus ex hac hominum frequentiā tolleret,: simulacra ex delubris,; so, pecunias e fano,: sphaeram ex urbe (Syracusis),: praedam,: posita,: patinam,; cf.: his sublatis,: mensam tolli jubet,: me per hostes Denso paventem sustulit aëre,: jubet sublata reponi Pocula,: cuncta,: tecum me tolle per undas,: me quoque tolle simul,: tollite me, Libyes, comitem poenaeque necisque,.—
In partic.
Pregn., to take off, carry off, make away with, to kill, destroy, ruin, etc.: aliquem de medio,: aliquem e medio,: aliquem ferro, veneno,: Titanas fulmine (Juppiter),: quem febris una potuit tollere, Lucil. ap. : me truncus illapsus cerebro Sustulerat, nisi, etc.,: tollet anum vitiato melle cicuta,: sorbitio tollit quem dira cicutae,: majores nostri Carthaginem et Numantiam funditus sustulerunt,laid waste,: ademptus Hector Tradidit fessis leviora tolli Pergama Graiis,.—In a play with I. B. supra: te dixisse, laudandum adulescentem (Caesarem), ornandum, tollendum, Brut. ap. ; cf.: se non esse commissurum, ut tolli posset,.—
Milit. t. t.: tollere signa, to break up for marching, to decamp, ; Auct. B. Alex. 57, 1.—
Trop., to do away with, remove; to abolish, annul, abrogate, cancel (very freq., esp. in Cic.; syn.: oblittero, aboleo): rei memoriam tollere ac delere,; cf. metum,: sublatā benevolentiā amicitiae nomen tollitur,; cf.: maximum ornamentum amicitiae tollit, qui ex eā tollit verecundiam,: dubitationem,: errorem,: librariorum menda,: ut id nomen ex omnibus libris tollatur,: legem,: veteres leges novis legibus,: dictaturam funditus ex re publicā,: sublato Areopago,: deos,to deny the existence of,; : diem,to consume in speechmaking,; : morbus facile tollitur,is removed,; ; so, dolores et tumores,: foeditates cicatricum maculasque,: muliebrem luctum,: querelas,.—Hence, sublātus, a, um, P. a. (acc. to I. B.), elated, proud, haughty (rare): quo proelio sublati Helvetii,: hac victoriā,: quibus omnibus rebus, id. B. C. 2, 37: rebus secundis,: gloriā, et saep.: fidens magis et sublatior ardet,. — Adv.: sublātē, highly, loftily. *
Lit.: Nilus diebus centum sublatius fluens, minuitur postea,higher,. —
Trop.: sublate ampleque dicere (opp. attenuate presseque),loftily, with elevation,: sublatius dicere,more proudly,: sublatius insolescentes,.

la:verb:torqueo.gloss: to spin, whirl, twirl, turn, cause to revolve
senses: to spin, whirl, twirl, turn, cause to revolve
to twist, wind, bend awry, distort
to hurl violently, twirl (around the head to throw), fling
la:verb:torqueo.html:
torquĕo, torsi, tortum, 2 (archaic
inf. torquerier, ), v. a.
Gr. τρέπω, to turn; cf. ἀτρεκής; also Sanscr. tarkus; Gr. ἄτρακτος, a spindle; and στρέφω, to twist
, to turn, turn about or away; to twist, bend, wind (class.; syn. converto).
Lit.
In gen.: cervices oculosque,: oculum,to roll, distort,: ora,to twist awry,: ab obscenis sermonibus aurem,: oculos ad moenia,: ad sonitum vocis vestigia,: serpens squamosos orbes Torquet,; cf. anguis,: capillos ferro,i. e. to curl, frizzle,: stamina pollice,: remis aquas,: spumas,: taxos in arcus,to bend,: tegumen torquens immane leonis,winding about him,: cum terra circum axem se convertat et torqueat,: torta circum bracchia vestis,.—
In partic.
To whirl around, to whirl in the act of throwing, to wield, brandish, to fling with force, to hurl (mostly poet.): torquet nunc lapidem, nunc ingens machina tignum,: amnis torquet sonantia saxa,: stuppea torquentem Balearis verbera fundae,: jaculum in hostem,; : hastam in hunc, id. ib 5, 137; for which: hastam alicui,: telum aurata ad tempora,: tela manu,: valido pila lacerto,: glebas, ramos,: cum fulmina torquet (Juppiter),; and trop.: cum Juppiter horridus austris Torquet aquosam hiemem,; cf.: Eurus nubes in occiduum orbem,.—In prose: torquere amentatas hastas lacertis,.—
To twist awry, misplace, turn aside, distort: negat sibi umquam, cum oculum torsisset, duas ex lucernā flammulas esse visas,: ora Tristia temptantum sensu (sapor) torquebit amaro,.—
To wrench the limbs upon the rack, to put to the rack or to the torture, to rack, torture (class.): ita te nervo torquebo, itidem uti catapultae solent,: eculeo torqueri,: aliquem servilem in modum,; cf.: ira torquentium,: servum in caput domini,against his master,: vinctus tortusve,

—

Trop.
In gen., to twist, wrest, distort, turn, bend, direct (a favorite expression of Cicero): versare suam naturam et regere ad tempus atque huc et illuc torquere ac flectere,: torquere et flectere imbecillitatem animorum,: oratio ita flexibilis, ut sequatur, quocumque torqueas,: omnia ad suae causae commodum,: verbo ac litterā jus omne torqueri,wrested, perverted,: sonum,to inflect,: cuncta tuo qui bella, pater, sub numine torques,: versare sententias, et huc atque illuc torquere,.—
In partic. (acc. to A. 2.), to rack, torment, torture (syn.: ango, crucio): tuae libidines te torquent,: mitto aurum coronarium, quod te diutissime torsit,: acriter nos tuae supplicationes torserunt, Cael. ap. : equidem dies noctesque torqueor,: verbi controversia jam diu torquet Graeculos homines,; : stulti malorum memoriā torquentur,: sollicitudine, poenitentia, etc., torquetur mens,: invidiā vel amore vigil torquebere,; : torqueor, infesto ne vir ab hoste cadat,; cf. : Aeacus torquet umbras,holds inquisition over,.—Transf.: (reges) dicuntur torquere mero, quem perspexisse laborant, qs. to rack with wine, i. e. to try or test with wine, ; so, vino tortus et irā,.—
To hurl, fling (of language): curvum sermone rotato enthymema,.—Hence, tortus, a, um, P. a., twisted, crooked, contorted, distorted.
Lit.: via (labyrinthi),quercus,i. e. a twisted oakgarland,.—Hence,
Subst.: torta, ae, f., a twisted loaf, a twist, . — *
Trop.: condiciones,confused, complicated,. —Adv.: tortē, awry, crookedly: torte penitusque remota, (329).

la:other:tot.html:
tŏt,
num. adj. indecl., so many.
Lit.
With a corresp. quot, quotiens, quantum, ut.
With quot: hoc brevissime dicam, neminem umquam tam impudentem fuisse, qui ab dis immortalibus tot et tantas res tacitus auderet optare, quot et quantas di immortales ad Cn. Pompeium detulerunt,: quot homines, tot causae,: qui tot annos, quot habet, designatus consul fuerit,, b, 2: quot haberet corpora pulvis, Tot mihi natales contingere vana rogavi,: tot mala sum passus, quot in aethere sidera lucent,.—
With quotiens: si tot consulibus meruisset, quotiens ipse consul fuisset,: si tot labores et pericula suscepissem, quotiens ductu meo hostes fusi, Dietsch. —
With quantum: quantum putabis ei rei satis esse, tot vites ablaqueato,. —
With ut: quae cum viderem tot vestigiis impressa, ut in his errari non posset,.—
Absol.
In connection with adjj. or advv. of kindred meaning, so many, so great a number: reliquae tot et tantae et tam graves civitates,; so, tot tantaeque difficultates,; and: in his tot et tantis malis,; cf. : tot viri ac tales,: tot ac tam validae manus,: tot, tam valida oppida,: ad haec tot tam inopinata incerti stupentesque,; repeated: ille cultus tot nobilium virorum, tot illustrium feminarum,.—
Alone, the correl.-clause being implied from the context, so many, such a great number, so very many: en excetra tu, quae tibi amicos tot habes,: nunc domi nostrae tot pessumi vivunt,: tot me impediunt curae,: cum tot signis eadem natura declaret, quid velit,; : ex centum quattuor centuriis, tot enim reliquae sunt (centuriae), etc.,: tot civitatum conjuratio,: unde tot hostes subito exorti,: tot caede procorum Admonitus non est,: cum tot curis regem videret urgeri,.—Rarely without a subst.: an timebant, ne tot unum ... superare non possent?: ex tot in Atridā pars quota laudis erat?.— With omnes: tot omnibus saeculis,.—
Transf.
To designate an optional, indefinite number, so many, such and such a number: volo dari ei, qui id egerit, a ceteris heredibus aureos tot,. —
As a relative numeral, also, for so few: vix credent tantum rerum cepisse tot annos,.

la:adj:tolerabilis.html:
tŏlĕrābĭlis, e, adj.
tolero
.
Pass., that may be borne, bearable, supportable, endurable, passable, tolerable (class.): amicitiae si tolerabiles erunt, ferendae sunt,: tolerabilis conditio servitutis,: genus rei publicae,: fenus,: hoc utcumque tolerabile: gravius illud quod, etc.,: regi tolerabili, aut, si vultis, etiam amabili,; cf. orator,: oratores,: Minucius jam ante vix tolerabilis,: non tolerabile numen,: habitus,.—Comp.: senectus,: tolerabilius est sic dicere, etc.,.—Sup.: sententia,. —
Act., that can easily bear or endure, enduring, sustaining, supporting (rare; not in Cic.; but cf. tolerabiliter, 2.): homo,: quas (oves) ille tempore auctumni ratus adhuc esse tolerabiles,i. e. able to support the winter,.—Adv.: tŏlĕrābĭ-lĭter.
Bearably, passably, tolerably: facere aliquid,: dicere,: dare veratrum,.—
For toleranter, patiently: etenim si dolores eosdem tolerabilius patiuntur,; so, tolerabilius ferre igniculum desiderii,.

la:verb:tolero.gloss: to bear, endure, tolerate, put up with, support
senses: to bear, endure, tolerate, put up with, support
to sustain (with the notion of barely doing so)
la:verb:tolero.html:
tŏlĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (
dep. collat. form tŏlĕror, āri, acc. to P.) [lengthened form of the root tol, whence tollo and tuli, kindr. with the Gr. ΤΛΑΩ], to bear, support, sustain (syn.: fero, patior, sustineo, sino).
Lit. (rare and mostly post-class.): aquilae ipsae non tolerantes pondus apprehensum una merguntur,; cf. : aliquem sinu,: gremio suo,, p. 154, 23: mensula cenae totius honestas reliquias tolerans,, p. 121, 26.—
Trop., to bear, endure, tolerate, sustain, support: militiam,: hiemem,; : dicunt illi dolorem esse difficile toleratu,: sumptus et tributa civitatum ab omnibus tolerari aequabiliter,: acritudinem, Att. ap. ; : facile labores pericula, dubias atque asperas res,: aequo animo servitutem,: cursus,: vaporem,; cf.: vaporis vim,: tanta peditum equitatumque vis damnaque et injuriae aegre tolerabantur,: sitim aestumque,.— Absol.: paulo longius tolerari posse,: posse ipsam Liviam statuere, nubendum post Drusum an in penatibus isdem tolerandum haberet,continue, remain,.—
With object-clause (poet. and in post - Aug. prose): ferro se caedi quam dictis his toleraret, Enn. ap. Müll. (Ann. v. 137 Vahl.): qui perpeti medicinam toleraverant,: magnitudinem mali perferre visu non toleravit, —
Of inanim. or abstr. subjects: Germania imbres tempestatesque tolerat,; : tolerat et annos metica (vitis),.—
Transf., to support a person or thing, i. e. to nourish, maintain, sustain, preserve by food, wealth, etc., = sustentare (v. h. v. II. B. 1.; so not in Cic.): his rationibus equitatum tolerare,: octona milia equitum suā pecuniā,: equos,: corpora equorum,; : se fructibus agri,: semetipsos (pisces clausi),: vitam,; ; : aevum,: annos,: egestatem,; so : paupertatem,: famem,: inopiam,.—Absol.: ut toleret (sc. erum amantem servus), ne pessum abeat,.—
To keep, observe: silentium obnixum,.— Hence,
tŏlĕrans, antis, P.a., bearing, supporting, enduring, tolerating, tolerant (post-Aug.; mostly with gen.): corpus laborum tolerans,: piscium genera dulcis undae tolerantia,. —Comp.: vacca frigoris tolerantior,: bello tolerantior,. —Sup.: asellus plagarum et penuriae tolerantissimus,.—Adv.: tŏlĕran-ter.
Patiently, enduringly, tolerantly: ferre aliquid,: pati dolorem,.—*
For tolerabiliter, bearably, tolerably: at nunc anniculae fecunditatem poscuntur, tolerantius tamen bimae,moderately,.—
tŏlĕrātus, a, um, P. a., supportable, tolerable: ut clementiam ac justitiam, quanto ignara barbaris, tanto toleratiora capesseret,acceptable,.† † toles (tolles), ĭum, m.
Celtic
, a wen on the neck, goitre, ; ; ; ; cf. Müll.

la:adj:togatus.html:
tŏgātus, a, um, adj.
toga
,
wearing the toga, clad in the toga, gowned: fovebit Romanos, rerum dominos, gentemque togatam,: ut togatus mandata senatus audiret,.—
Transf., of a private station: sportula turbae rapienda togatae, by the crowd of clients (cf. toga, II. B. 2.), : opera,the service of a client,. — Hence, subst.
tŏgātus, i, m., lit., a Roman citizen, opp. to a foreigner or to a Roman soldier: judex modo palliatus modo togatus,: cui uni togato supplicationem decreverit (senatus),: unus e togatorum numero,: magna caterva togatorum,: crudelitas in togatos,to Romans,: non pudet lictorum vestrorum majorem prope numerum in foro conspici quam togatorum?: inter togatos,; .— In the time of the emperors togati seems to have been the designation of the citizens, in opposition to the plebs sordida, the tunicati,the third class,; cf. Roth in Jahn's Neues Jahrb. 1858, vol. 77, p. 286 sq.—
(Acc. to toga, II. B. 2.) Under the emperors, a man of humble station, a client, .—
tŏgāta, ae, f. (sc. fabula), a species of the Roman drama which treated of Roman subjects, the national drama, P.; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; cf. Com. Rel. p. 113 sq. Rib.—
(Acc. to toga, II. B. 3.) Togata, of an immodest woman, a prostitute: ancilla,; cf. ; .—
Esp.: Gallia Togata,the part of Gallia Cisalpina acquired by the Romans on the hither side of the Po,; ; ; .

senses: a client, man of humble station

la:verb:torreo.html:
torreo, torrui, tostum (
part. gen. plur. torrentum, ; ; abl. torrenti, ), 2, v. a.
Sanscr. tarsh, to thirst; Gr. τέρσομαι, to become dry; Germ. Durst.; Engl. thirst
, to dry a thing by heat, to parch, roast, bake, scorch, burn, etc. (syn. frigo): fruges receptas Et torrere parant flammis et frangere saxo,; ; : aristas sole novo,: pisces sole,: apes mortuas sole verno,: uvam in tegulis, et saep.; : etiamsi in Phalaridis tauro inclusus succensis ignibus torrebatur,: e quibus (terrae cingulis) medium illum et maximum solis ardore torreri, : cum undique flamma torrerentur,: montes quos torret Atabulus,; cf.: torrentia agros sidera,: tosti alti stant parietes, i. e. consumed, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 116 Vahl.): carmina flammā,: tostos en aspice crines,: in veribus exta,to roast,: aliquid in igne,: artus subjecto igni,: carnem, et saep.—Of fever heat, to dry up: at mihi (vae miserae) torrentur febribus artus,: febris viscera ipsa torrens,; .—Of thirst: et Canis arenti torreat arva siti,.—Of the heat of love: si torrere jecur quaeris idoneum (Venus),; cf.: correptus saevo Veneris torrebar aëno,: torret amor Cyri Lycorida,: me torret face mutuā Calais,: me amor Glycerae,: femineus pectora torret amor,.— *
Transf., of cold, to nip, pinch (cf. uro and aduro): frigore torret, Varr. ap. . — Hence, torrens, entis, P. a., in a neutr. sense, burning, hot, inflamed.
Lit. (rare): terra torrens aestu,: miles torrens meridiano sole,: Sirius,: flammae,.—Comp.: Sirius torrentior, 20.—Sup.: torrentissimus axis,.—
Transf., of streams, rushing, roaring, boiling, impetuous, rapid, etc. (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose): fluvii,: flumina,: Nilus toto gurgite,; cf.: fluvius Novanus solstitiis torrens,; : aqua,: unda,: torrentes rapidique cursus amnium,; : impetus (aquae),: sanguis,; cf. fatum,.—Comp.: Padus torrentior,.—Sup.: Asopos torrentissimus,.—Hence,
Subst.: torrens, entis, m., a torrent: cum fertur quasi torrens oratio,; ; : rapidus montano flumine torrens Sternit agros,: fragosus,; : tumidus,; ; ; .—Prov.: numquam direxit bracchia contra torrentem,. —
Transf.: armorum et virorum,: umbrarum,; cf. fortunae,.—

la:noun:torus.html:
tŏrus, i, m. (also tŏrum, i, n., Varr. ap. ; ) [for storus; root ster-, stra-, of sterno, stramen; Gr. στορέννυμι, to spread, scatter], prop.,
a round, swelling, or bulging place, an elevation, protuberance, prominence; hence,
A knot, bulge: (funis) : funiculorum,; cf.: vitis toris ad arborem religetur,: firmi vitis,.—
The muscular or fleshy part, the muscle, brawn of animal bodies (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose): o lacertorum tori! Cic. poët. Tusc. 2, 9, 22; ; ; ; 14, 283; 15, 230; : leo gaudet comantes Excutiens cervice toros,: luxuriatque toris animosum pectus,; ; ; ; : venarum tori,varicose dilatations of the veins, —

A raised ornament, a knot, on a garland; trop., of language: isque (stilus mediocris) uno tenore fluit, aut addit aliquos, ut in coronā, toros omnemque orationem ornamentis modicis verborum sententiarumque distinguit,.—
A bolster, cushion, so named from its protuberances; hence, a couch, sofa, bed (mostly poet.; syn.: stratum, lectus): antiquis torus e stramento erat, qualiter etiam nunc in castris,: viridante toro consederat herbae,; cf.: praebuit herba torum,; : datque torum caespes,: gramine vestitis accubuere toris,: silvestrem montana torum cum sterneret uxor Frondibus,: discumbere toris,.—So of a sofa: toro sic orsus ab alto,; .—Of a bed: ambierantque torum,: concutiuntque torum de molli fluminis ulvā Impositum lecto,: ebeno sublimis in atrā,; . — Of a corpse-bed, ; : membra toro defleta reponunt,.—Of a bridalbed, : (lectica) sive illa toro resupina feretur,; cf. Becker, Gallus, 2, p. 240 (2d ed.).—
Transf., like thalamus, as a designation for marriage: Deucalion ... Cum consorte tori,with his consort, spouse,; cf.: socia tori,; so ; 7, 332; ; ; : genialis,; : obscenus,i. e. illicit connection,; cf. illiciti (with stupra),: receptus in torum,.—Hence, also, for a mistress: torum donare alicui,.—
An elevation, bank of earth: riparum,; : pulvinorum,; .—
In architecture, a large, round moulding at the base of a column, a torus, .

senses: to speak thunderously, make a loud, thundering noise
la:verb:tono.html:
tŏno, ŭi, 1 (collat. form of third conj.: tonimus, Varr. ap. ), v. n. and a.
[root in Sanscr. tan-, to stretch, extend; Gr. τείνω; whence teneo, tendo, tenus; cf. O. H. Germ. donar; Engl. thunder], to thunder.
Lit.: ingens Porta tonat caeli, Enn. ap. Vet. Gram. ap. Col. (Ann. v. 597 Vahl.); imitated by : cum tonuit laevum bene tempestate serenā, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 517 Vahl.): ut valide tonuit!; so : si fulserit, si tonuerit,: Jove tonante,; : tonans Juppiter,; ; : sub axe tonanti Sternitur aequor,: pater nudā de rupe tonabat,nec si consulto fulmina missa tonent, (3, 32), 54: Diespiter per purum tonantes Egit equos,: Juppiter, tona,.—
Transf., in gen.
Neutr., to make a loud, thundering noise, to roar, rattle, crash, etc. (cf.: crepo, strepo): tympana tenta tonant,: Aetna horrificis ruinis,: caelum omne fragore,; cf. : domus afflicta massa,: nemus fragore vasto,; .—Of loud, thundering speech: Pericles fulgere, tonare, dictus est,; ; Col. praef. § 30: qualis Pindarico spiritus ore tonat, (4, 16), 40; .—
Act., to thunder forth, to say or name with a thundering voice: tercentum tonat ore deos,invokes with thundering voice,: verba foro,aspera bella,: talia celso ore,: Cicerona,.—Hence, P. a., as epithet of Jupiter: Tŏnans, antis, m., the thunderer, god of thunder, ; ; ; ; ; cf.: Capitolinus Tonans,: sceptriferi Tonantes, Jupiter and Juno,.—Also of Saturn: falcifer Tonans,.

As a designation for peace: ex quo genere haec sunt, Liberum appellare pro vino, campum pro comitiis, togam pro pace, arma ac tela pro bello,: cedant arma togae, id. poët. Off. 1, 22, 77; : vir omnibus belli ac togae dotibus eminens,; .—Also of the Roman national character; hence, togae oblitus, forgetful of Rome, .—
As, in the times of the emperors, the toga went more and more out of use, and became almost exclusively the garment of clients, poet. for a client: eheu quam fatuae sunt tibi Roma togae,; ; cf. ; . —
As women of loose character were not allowed to wear the proper female garment (the stola), and assumed the toga, poet. for a prostitute: si tibi cura togae est

potior pressumque quasillo Scortum, .
